key_facts: *Candida* (mostly *C. albicans*) infection of **warm, moist skin folds**.
**Beefy red**, macerated fold with **satellite papules and pustules** at the edge; may involve the scrotum.
Risk factors: obesity, diabetes, sweating, occlusion, incontinence, antibiotics, steroids, immunosuppression.
Treat with **moisture control** plus a topical imidazole (e.g. clotrimazole) until 1–2 weeks after clearance; hydrocortisone 1% short term if inflamed.
Recurrent or extensive: check **HbA1c**, review drugs and consider swabs.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Candidal intertrigo is a **yeast infection of moist skin folds**, usually caused by *Candida albicans*. Common sites are under the breasts, under an abdominal apron, the groin, the axillae and the finger or toe webs (*erosio interdigitalis blastomycetica*).

**Intertrigo** itself is inflammation of the skin folds from heat, moisture, friction and poor ventilation. Secondary Candida infection is common, and **satellite papules and pustules** are the key diagnostic clue.

sub: Common at both ends of life: **infants** (napkin area) and older, less mobile adults.
More common in hot, humid weather and in people with obesity or diabetes.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: *Candida* is an **opportunist**. It overgrows where skin is wet, warm, occluded and macerated.

ul: **Diabetes** (look for it)
Recent **antibiotics** or systemic steroids
Immunosuppression
Obesity and deep skin folds
Incontinence, nappies and pads
Wet work, for finger-web disease
**Local**: heat, moisture, friction, occlusive clothing, incontinence, poor hygiene of folds.
**Systemic**: **diabetes**, obesity, broad-spectrum antibiotics, systemic or topical steroids, immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy), pregnancy.
**"All fold rashes are thrush"**: irritant intertrigo, flexural psoriasis, erythrasma and tinea cruris look similar.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: *Candida* is a normal commensal that becomes invasive when **local moisture or host defences** change.

mech.t: Sweat and friction macerate the stratum corneum in folds, weakening the barrier (irritant intertrigo).
Commensal *Candida* multiplies in the warm, wet fold and adheres using surface adhesins.
mech.caption: A macerated skin fold with Candida yeasts and hyphae invading the softened stratum corneum.

mech.t: Yeasts switch to **pseudohyphae and hyphae**, releasing proteases and phospholipases that invade the stratum corneum and trigger neutrophil inflammation.
Small pustules and papules form beyond the main edge where yeasts seed new follicles: the **satellite** sign.

histo: Yeasts and pseudohyphae in the stratum corneum (PAS stain) with neutrophils and subcorneal pustules.
Diagnosis is clinical; swab or scrape for microscopy and culture if unsure or recurrent.

ul: **Beefy-red, macerated plaques** in folds, often glistening or eroded.
**Satellite papules and pustules** beyond the main edge. This is the key sign.
Peripheral peeling scale at the margin.
Soreness, itch or burning.
In the groin, Candida often **involves the scrotum**, which tinea tends to spare.

blocks.title: Look elsewhere
blocks.text: Candidal intertrigo can coexist with oral or genital thrush, so ask and examine.

sections.title: Management

blocks.h: Moisture control: the most important step

ul: Dry the folds thoroughly after washing (pat dry, or use a cool hairdryer).
Use absorbent interface textiles or cotton separators. Choose barrier products for incontinence.
Wear loose cotton clothing, and give weight-management advice where relevant.
**Imidazole** (clotrimazole or miconazole) or **nystatin**. Continue until 1–2 weeks after clearance.

For very inflamed folds, a short course of a combination with mild steroid (e.g. hydrocortisone with clotrimazole or miconazole) is sometimes used. Follow the local formulary and limit to about 7 days.

blocks: **Fluconazole** for severe or recalcitrant disease. Check interactions and pregnancy status.

blocks.h: Look for and treat the cause

blocks: Review for diabetes, recent antibiotics and immunosuppression.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Find the cause**: Review diabetes, antibiotics, immunosuppression.
**Toe webs**: Often mixed yeast, dermatophyte and bacteria: dry thoroughly plus the right antimicrobial.

refer.t: Spreading **cellulitis**, fever or systemically unwell: escalate.
Recurrent or extensive: **screen for diabetes**, consider immunosuppression.
No response to an adequate course: rethink (psoriasis, tinea, erythrasma) and sample.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Recurrent or extensive candida: **screen for diabetes** and consider immunosuppression.
No response to an adequate course: reconsider the diagnosis (psoriasis, tinea, erythrasma) and take samples.
Spreading cellulitis, fever or a systemically unwell patient: escalate.
Secondary bacterial infection; fissuring and pain.
Spread to other folds, nails (chronic paronychia) or mouth.
Persistent post-inflammatory pigmentation.
Responds well to treatment, but **recurs** unless moisture and risk factors are controlled.

pearls: **Satellites mean Candida.** No satellites and a very sharp edge suggests flexural psoriasis.
Treatment fails without moisture control. Make the drying advice practical and specific.
OTC clotrimazole is a sensible first pharmacy intervention for limited disease.
In finger-web disease, ask about wet work and rings.
The toe-web ‘dermatophytosis complex’ is often a **mixed** yeast, dermatophyte and bacterial picture. It needs thorough drying plus the right antimicrobial.
KOH-negative fold rash, or one that keeps coming back? Work through [intertrigo and the flexural differential](condition:intertrigo).
